\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
Yet feeding thousands of trace lines to a model can be no better than feeding none: the diagnostic signal drowns in routine execution steps.
\emph{Which trace components actually carry the signal that matters?}

Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks.
\emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, enabling controlled component ablation.
As fault detection, the model need not simulate execution, only determine whether something went wrong---and if that signal is concentrated in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.

We test this hypothesis through the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2025coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.
The results are striking: complete traces (${\sim}$80\%) underperform a single compact component (${\geq}$99\%) despite containing strictly more information---a direct demonstration that information density, not quantity, determines learning efficiency.

\textbf{Exception events alone achieve ${\geq}$99.83\% verdict accuracy on three of four models (${\geq}$99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds; CodeLlama-13B seed 123 reaches 100\%).}
DeepSeek-6.7B is the exception: its 3-seed mean is 96.58\% ($\pm$4.76pp) due to one seed exhibiting format collapse (fail recall = 70.5\%), though even this outlier outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp.
This near-perfect accuracy holds from 1.5B to 13B parameters, while the code-only baseline (\texttt{no\_trace}) varies from 67.3\% to 76.5\% with strong scale dependence.
Training dynamics expose the mechanism (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}): \texttt{exception\_only} converges to 99.33\% within 50 training steps and saturates at 99.83\% by step 150, while even \texttt{full\_trace} with label-only loss (gradient dilution eliminated) oscillates between 82\% and 89\% across the entire training without stable convergence, consistent with overfitting to spurious patterns in verbose content.

Adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit and can degrade performance: VOTA (3-seed mean 99.05\%) underperforms \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) on Qwen-7B, with the gap reaching 14.96pp on DeepSeek due to tokenizer-driven truncation.
The performance gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\sim}$76\%) and gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) on Qwen-7B (3 seeds).
A tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens, with \texttt{tail\_2048} recovering 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy.
Even on silent logic errors (55.5\% of failures), \texttt{exception\_only} maintains 100\% recall because test assertions generate exception events.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Information density determines SFT learning efficiency}: training dynamics directly show that denser trace components learn faster and more stably---\texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} with label-only loss oscillates (82--89\%) without stable convergence. Seed variance negatively correlates with input density ($\sigma{=}$0.00 to 1.12), and SFT closes a 6--49pp zero-shot gap across all models (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
\item \textbf{Exception events are the minimal sufficient signal}: ${\geq}$99.83\% on three of four models, ${\geq}$99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds (1.5B--13B, three families), with ${\sim}$91\% semantic rather than format-driven (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}, \S\ref{sec:nomarker}). Cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the ranking, though margins narrow from ceiling effects (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).
\item \textbf{Approximate density decomposition (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds)}: The performance gap decomposes into gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) and information overload (${\sim}$76\%), implying content selection matters more than loss engineering. A budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tail tokens (\S\ref{sec:density}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy (Qwen-7B; cross-model verification in progress)}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertions) individually achieve ${\geq}$99\%; Tier~2 (loop compression) reaches 86.1\%, still +10.9pp over no trace (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Method}
2	
3	\subsection{Task Definition}
4	
5	We study \emph{verdict prediction}: given a Python function, a test input, and an optional execution trace, predict whether the test passes or fails.
6	The model produces a single token (\texttt{pass} or \texttt{fail}), making this a binary classification task.
7	Unlike code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile} or output prediction \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, verdict prediction isolates the model's ability to detect faults from its ability to simulate execution.
8	The discrete binary outcome makes the effect of each trace component directly measurable, providing cleaner ablation contrasts than generation tasks where output quality varies continuously.
9	
10	\subsection{Dataset}
11	\label{sec:dataset}
12	
13	We sampled 10 candidate solutions per problem from Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (temperature 0.8, top\_p 0.95) for 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} (164) and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program} (427), executed each against canonical tests with \texttt{sys.settrace} to obtain line-level traces and pass/fail verdicts, yielding 5,910 pairs (67\% pass, 33\% fail).
14	The dataset is split 80/20 by problem ID into 4,720 training and 1,190 test samples (majority baseline: 71.51\%).
15	The \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (39.45\% train, 48.99\% test duplicates); these duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem, with the train--test split enforced at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}).
16	
17	\subsection{Trace Representations}
18	
19	We define seven conditions that vary the trace information available (Figure~\ref{fig:trace_overview}):
20	\begin{itemize}
21	\item \texttt{no\_trace}: Source code and test input only.
22	\item \texttt{full\_trace}: Complete line-by-line trace with variable states.
23	\item \texttt{VOTA}: Exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression (Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_algorithm}).
24	\item \texttt{exception\_only}: Only exception/error events.
25	\item \texttt{ae\_only}: Only assertion-point actual/expected pairs.
26	\item \texttt{loop\_only}: Only loop compression summaries.
27	\item \texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae}: VOTA without assertion-point information.
28	\end{itemize}
29	
30	\begin{figure*}[t]
31	\centering
32	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig1_trace_overview}
33	\caption{Overview of the verdict prediction pipeline. Source code and a test input are executed to produce a full raw trace. Four conditions vary the trace information: \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%), \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%), VOTA (99.41\%), and \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%). Accuracies for Qwen-2.5-7B (seed=42, $N{=}1{,}190$). Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_examples} provides input/output examples.}
34	\label{fig:trace_overview}
35	\end{figure*}
36	
37	\subsection{Models and Training}
38	
39	We evaluate four models spanning three architecture families: \textbf{Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct} \citep{qwen2025coder}, \textbf{CodeLlama-13B-Instruct} \citep{roziere2024code}, and \textbf{DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct} \citep{deepseek2024coder}, covering a 1.5B--13B parameter range (8.7$\times$).
40	All conditions use LoRA \citep{hu2022lora} (rank=16, $\alpha$=32, dropout=0.05) on all linear layers, 3 epochs, effective batch size 32, LR $2 \times 10^{-4}$ with linear warmup/decay, max sequence length 2{,}048 tokens.
41	Sequences exceeding this limit are truncated while preserving the verdict label.
42	The primary seed is 42; seeds 123 and 456 test \texttt{exception\_only} robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_details}).
43	
44	\subsection{Loss Ablation}
45	
46	To disentangle training signal from input signal quality, we introduce \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only}: identical full-trace input but loss computed only on the verdict token (trace positions masked).
47	Improvement over standard \texttt{full\_trace} is attributable to \emph{gradient dilution}; the remaining gap to VOTA reflects \emph{information overload} at inference time.
48

1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	We evaluate across two research questions:
4	(1)~Do Tier~1 exception signals generalize across models?
5	(2)~What is the relative contribution of each trace component?
6	All experiments use $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% CIs.\footnote{Data is partitioned at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; \S\ref{sec:dataset}). The \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (48.99\% test duplicates; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}), but these arise from within-problem variants, not cross-set leakage; deduplication sensitivity analysis confirms 0.00pp delta across all 19 experimental conditions.}
7	Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, seed=42); all differences are significant at $p{<}0.0001$ unless noted.
8	
9	\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
10	\label{sec:cross_model}
11	
12	Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} compares four models spanning an 8.7$\times$ parameter range (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families (Qwen, DeepSeek, CodeLlama) under key conditions.
13	
14	\begin{table}[t]
15	\centering
16	\caption{Cross-model verdict accuracy (\%, $N{=}1{,}190$) across four models (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families. Multi-seed entries report mean$\pm$std over 3 seeds. Bold: best per model. Full per-seed breakdowns in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}; per-class metrics in Appendix~\ref{sec:per_class}.}
17	\label{tab:cross_model}
18	\small
19	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
20	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
21	\toprule
22	\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Qwen-7B} & \textbf{Qwen-1.5B} & \textbf{CL-13B} & \textbf{DS-6.7B} \\
23	\midrule
24	exception\_only & \textbf{99.83}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & \textbf{99.83}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & \textbf{99.89}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.10} & \textbf{99.33}$^\dag$ \\
25	ae\_only & 99.64{\scriptsize$\pm$0.49} & --- & --- & --- \\
26	VOTA & 99.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.38} & 99.58 & 98.57 & 84.45 \\
27	no\_trace & 75.13 & 67.31 & 76.47 & 73.36 \\
28	\midrule
29	Majority baseline & \multicolumn{4}{c}{71.51} \\
30	\bottomrule
31	\end{tabular}%
32	}
33	\vspace{2pt}
34	\par\raggedright\footnotesize
35	$^\dag$DeepSeek 3-seed mean 96.58\%$\pm$4.76pp; seed 123 (91.09\%, fail recall\,=\,70.5\%) exhibits format collapse on long inputs (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}), reported as 2-seed mean excluding the outlier.
36	VOTA on Qwen-7B: 99.41/98.66/99.08 ($\sigma{=}$0.38).
37	\texttt{ae\_only} 3 seeds: 99.92/99.08/99.92 (mean 99.64\%); \texttt{loop\_only}: 85.63/85.88/86.64 (mean 86.05\%).
38	Qwen-1.5B \texttt{exception\_only}: 99.83\% across 3 seeds ($\sigma{=}$0).
39	\end{table}
40	
41	\paragraph{Exception dominance across families.}
42	Under \texttt{exception\_only}, the Qwen and CodeLlama families achieve ${\geq}$99.83\% (mean): Qwen-7B (99.83\%$\pm$0.00, 3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B (99.83\%), and CodeLlama-13B (99.89\%$\pm$0.10, 3 seeds; seed 123 achieves 100\%).
43	DeepSeek-6.7B reaches 99.33\% on 2/3 seeds with one LoRA-sensitivity outlier at 91.09\% (seed 123; fail recall = 70.5\%); even the outlier outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp.
44	Excluding the DeepSeek outlier, the cross-model range is 0.56pp (99.33--99.89\%), the tightest of any condition.
45	
46	\paragraph{Scale invariance of exception signals.}
47	Exception-based accuracy is shared by models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters (8.7$\times$): both Qwen-1.5B and CodeLlama-13B achieve 99.83\%+ on the same representation.
48	CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% (0/1190 errors), confirming that Qwen's two persistent errors (from \texttt{GeneratorExit}; Appendix~\ref{sec:irreducible}) are high-probability convergence artifacts rather than hard data limitations.
49	In contrast, \texttt{no\_trace} scales monotonically with capacity: 67.31\% (1.5B) $\to$ 75.13\% (7B) $\to$ 76.47\% (13B), a 9.16pp range that exception events completely eliminate (Figure~\ref{fig:cross_scale}).
50	
51	\begin{figure}[t]
52	\centering
53	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_cross_model_gap}
54	\caption{Verdict accuracy vs.\ model scale. \texttt{exception\_only} maintains ${\geq}$99.33\% regardless of scale (1.5B--13B), while \texttt{no\_trace} shows monotonic scale sensitivity (+9.16pp from 1.5B to 13B). The \texttt{nomarker} condition (format markers removed) shows no degradation at smaller scale (${\sim}$97.7--97.8\%).}
55	\label{fig:cross_scale}
56	\end{figure}
57	
58	\paragraph{VOTA cross-family variation.}
59	VOTA accuracy varies across families: 99.58\% (Qwen-1.5B) $>$ 99.05\%$\pm$0.38 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) $>$ 98.57\% (CodeLlama-13B; CI [97.9, 99.2]) $\gg$ 84.45\% (DeepSeek-6.7B).
60	The CodeLlama result (17 errors) narrows the gap: among models without tokenizer-driven truncation, the VOTA range is only 1.01pp (98.57--99.58\%), suggesting that the 14.96pp DeepSeek deficit is primarily a truncation artifact rather than an inherent model capability limitation (91.7\% of DeepSeek training samples were affected; Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).
61	In contrast, \texttt{exception\_only} inputs are compact (median 150 tokens, mean 398 due to verbose fail-class exceptions), making the cross-model comparison clean (Appendix~\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}).
62	
63	\subsection{Component Ablation}
64	\label{sec:ablation}
65	
66	We restrict \texttt{ae\_only} and \texttt{loop\_only} ablations to Qwen-7B, as these component-level analyses target the trace composition mechanism rather than cross-model generalization.
67	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} decomposes VOTA on Qwen-2.5-7B and reveals a two-tier hierarchy on this model; the cross-model consistency of \texttt{exception\_only} (${\geq}$99.33\% on all four models) suggests Tier~1 generalizes, though direct Tier~2 verification on other models remains future work.
68	
69	\begin{table}[t]
70	\centering
71	\caption{Component ablation on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$). Tier~1 signals achieve near-perfect accuracy; combining them (VOTA) slightly dilutes performance. $^\dag$\texttt{ae\_only}: 3-seed mean 99.64\%$\pm$0.49 (seeds 42/123/456: 99.92/99.08/99.92). \texttt{exception\_only}: 99.83\%$\pm$0.00 (3 seeds). $^\S$VOTA: 3-seed mean 99.05\%$\pm$0.38 (99.41/98.66/99.08). $^\ddag$\texttt{loop\_only}: 3-seed mean 86.05\%$\pm$0.52 (85.63/85.88/86.64). Seed variance negatively correlates with information density: $\sigma{=}$0.00 (exception) ${<}$ 0.38 (VOTA) ${<}$ 0.49 (ae) ${<}$ 0.52 (loop).}
72	\label{tab:ablation}
73	\small
74	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
75	\begin{tabular}{llccc}
76	\toprule
77	\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Components} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Tier} \\
78	\midrule
79	ae\_only & assertion-point & 99.64$^\dag$ & [99.26, 99.87] & 1 \\
80	exception\_only & exception events & \textbf{99.83} & [99.58, 100.00] & 1 \\
81	VOTA & exc+ae+loop & 99.05$^\S$ & [98.49, 99.50] & --- \\
82	VOTA\_no\_ae & exc+loop & 99.41 & [98.90, 99.80] & --- \\
83	loop\_only & loop compression & 86.05$^\ddag$ & [83.97, 87.96] & 2 \\
84	full\_trace & complete trace & 81.76 & [79.70, 83.90] & --- \\
85	no\_trace & none & 75.13 & [72.77, 77.48] & --- \\
86	\midrule
87	Regex (best) & exc.\ type regex & 93.61 & --- & --- \\
88	3-shot (Qwen-7B) & in-context learning & 90.84 & --- & --- \\
89	Zero-shot (4 models) & prompting & 51.0--93.5 & --- & --- \\
90	\bottomrule
91	\end{tabular}%
92	}
93	\end{table}
94	
95	Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%$\pm$0.00) exceeds VOTA (99.05\%$\pm$0.38) by +0.78pp (2/3 seeds $p{<}0.05$, all directionally consistent), implying that combining signals introduces noise.
96	Removing assertion points has no effect (\texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae} = 99.41\%, single seed), confirming exception dominance.
97	Tier~2 \texttt{loop\_only} (86.05\%, 3-seed mean) improves 10.92pp over \texttt{no\_trace} ($p{<}0.0001$) but falls far short of Tier~1.
98	\paragraph{Rule-based baseline comparison.}
99	The strongest non-trivial regex heuristic (B4: exception class name matching; Table~\ref{tab:regex}) achieves 93.61\% accuracy (F1=0.876), trailing SFT \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%, F1=0.997) by 6.22pp (McNemar $p{<}0.001$).
100	The gap concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases: regex flags all exception events as failures, while SFT learns to distinguish caught exceptions (benign, inside \texttt{try/except}) from uncaught faults, correctly resolving 6/8 boundary samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
101	Across trace formats, SFT consistently outperforms the best applicable regex, from +3.62pp (\texttt{no\_trace} over majority baseline) to +23.86pp (VOTA), with the largest gains on formats requiring semantic interpretation (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
102	
103	\paragraph{Zero-shot and few-shot LLM baselines.}
104	Zero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\% across four models (42.44pp range), with performance uncorrelated with model size (Qwen-1.5B: 93.45\% vs.\ CodeLlama-13B: 51.01\%).
105	Three-shot ICL on Qwen-7B (90.84\%) improves only 1.76pp and still trails SFT by 8.99pp.
106	SFT compresses this 42.44pp range to 0.56pp (99.33--99.89\%), closing a 6--49pp gap with 4,720 training samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}).
107	
108	\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
109	\label{sec:nomarker}
110	
111	The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
112	To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).
113	
114	Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
115	Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.
116	The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).
117	Exception events thus provide two signal layers that show no degradation at smaller scale: structural markers (${\sim}$2pp, regex-learnable) and semantic exception content (${\sim}$22pp, requiring SFT to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions).
118	
119	\subsection{Information Density Decomposition}
120	\label{sec:density}
121	
122	The 17.29pp gap between \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) and VOTA (99.05\%, 3-seed mean) decomposes via \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only} (85.94\%$\pm$1.12, 3 seeds; Table~\ref{tab:density}), which retains the full trace but masks all trace tokens from the loss.

125	\centering
126	\caption{Approximate information density decomposition: gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) vs.\ information overload (${\sim}$76\%). \texttt{label\_only} and VOTA are 3-seed means on Qwen-7B.}
127	\label{tab:density}
128	\small
129	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
130	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
131	\toprule
132	\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ vs.\ full\_trace} & \textbf{Gap explained} \\
133	\midrule

135	label\_only & 85.94{\scriptsize$\pm$1.12} & +4.18pp & 24\% \\

141	
142	Gradient dilution accounts for approximately 24\% of the gap (+4.18pp, 3-seed mean): when the model no longer wastes gradient updates on predicting trace tokens, accuracy improves even with identical input.
143	The remaining ${\sim}$76\% (+13.11pp) reflects information overload at inference: the model receives thousands of irrelevant trace lines that compete for attention with the diagnostic signal, regardless of loss design.
144	This asymmetry implies that trace compression methods should prioritize \emph{content selection} (removing irrelevant lines) over \emph{loss engineering} (masking non-target tokens), as the larger bottleneck is what the model sees, not how it is trained.
145	The two factors may interact, so this decomposition is approximate.
146	Label-only loss simultaneously changes multiple optimization dynamics (effective gradient norm, implicit regularization from trace token prediction); the 24\%/76\% attribution should be interpreted as an approximate decomposition rather than a strict causal partition.
147	This analysis uses 3 seeds on a single model (Qwen-7B); cross-model validation remains future work.
148	
149	\subsection{Additional Analyses}
150	\label{sec:additional}
151	
152	\paragraph{Trace length ablation.}
153	\label{sec:trace_length}
154	Varying the head-truncated trace token budget (256--no limit) on Qwen-7B yields accuracy in a narrow 77.2\%--81.8\% band with a non-monotonic pattern: 1024-token prefixes (77.23\%) underperform 512-token prefixes (80.42\%, $p{=}0.002$), because mid-length prefixes retain enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events near the trace terminus (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
155	This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation; under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for two of three models (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model} in Appendix), with only DeepSeek showing a mild architecture-specific reversal at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048 ($-$1.5pp).
156	
157	\paragraph{Truncation direction and budget curve.}
158	Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: among the three models with complete data, tail-2048 exceeds head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp, with the gap widening at smaller scale (Qwen-1.5B: +22.6pp vs.\ Qwen-7B: +15.5pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}, Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail}).
159	All four models' head-2048 accuracies converge into a narrow 75.3--81.8\% band (6.5pp), comparable to the tail-256 band (72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp), indicating that signal-poor conditions produce a shared performance floor regardless of scale or architecture.
160	
161	A cross-model budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a phase transition localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens.
162	At tail-384, all models remain near baseline (73.6--82.9\%, only +1.0--6.5pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\to$512 (+11.0--22.0pp), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling (${\sim}$94--98\%).
163	This localizes the critical threshold to ${\sim}$400--500 tokens, matching the typical exception traceback length (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}).
164	Beyond 512 tokens, accuracy converges further: multi-seed validation across all 12 model$\times$seed combinations confirms all tail-512 accuracies fall within a 4.63pp band [93.61\%, 98.24\%] (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}); at tail-1024, three models reach 96.5--98.2\%, compressing the 6.3pp cross-model spread observed at tail-256.
165	\texttt{tail\_2048} captures 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy across all completed configurations.
166	The residual 2--5pp gap confirms that semantic extraction (identifying exception type and message) still outperforms positional extraction (retaining a fixed window containing non-diagnostic lines).
167	
168	\paragraph{Calibration.}
169	\label{sec:calibration}
170	Calibration mirrors the tier hierarchy: \texttt{exception\_only} achieves ECE = 0.0027 vs.\ 0.171 for \texttt{no\_trace}, a 63$\times$ gap (Figure~\ref{fig:calibration}).
171	This calibration advantage generalizes across models: all three tested architectures achieve ECE ${<}$ 0.007 under \texttt{exception\_only} (Appendix~\ref{sec:calibration_full}).
172	
173	\paragraph{Error orthogonality.}
174	\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors have zero overlap with all other conditions' error sets (Jaccard = 0.000), confirming it operates on an independent signal dimension (Appendix~\ref{sec:error_overlap}).
175	
176	\paragraph{Exception type breakdown.}
177	A per-exception-type breakdown (Appendix~\ref{sec:exception_type}) confirms that all standard exception types achieve 100\% accuracy; the only failures arise from \texttt{GeneratorExit}, a benign \texttt{BaseException} subclass.
178	
179	\paragraph{Cross-dataset generalization.}
180	\label{sec:debugbench}
181	On DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench} ($N{=}426$), the ranking is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} 100\%, VOTA 99.77\%, \texttt{no\_trace} 96.71\%; narrow margins reflect a ceiling effect from structurally distinctive mutations (Appendix~\ref{sec:debugbench_full}).
182

102	\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
103	\label{sec:vota_algorithm}
104	
105	Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.
106	
107	\begin{algorithm}[t]
108	\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
109	\label{alg:vota}
110	\small
111	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
112	\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
113	\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
114	\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
115	\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
116	\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
117	  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
118	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
119	\ENDFOR
120	\IF{no exception events found}
121	  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
122	\ENDIF
123	\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
124	\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
125	  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
126	  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
127	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
128	\ENDFOR
129	\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
130	\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
131	  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
132	    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
133	  \ENDIF
134	\ENDFOR
135	\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
136	\RETURN $V$
137	\end{algorithmic}
138	\end{algorithm}

250	\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
251	\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}
252	
253	The VOTA cross-model gap (14.96pp, Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}; confounded by tokenizer-driven truncation; 91.7\% of DeepSeek training samples were affected) is driven by a training-time truncation asymmetry.
254	The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
255	The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
256	
257	A post-hoc group analysis provides directional evidence: partitioning DeepSeek VOTA test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}0.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
258	Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that DeepSeek VOTA achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}, in contrast to Qwen VOTA, which achieves 100\% fail recall.
259	
260	Seed robustness diverges across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), while DeepSeek shows bimodal behavior: seeds 42 and 456 achieve 99.33\% (fail recall = 100\%), seed 123 yields 91.09\% (fail recall = 70.5\%).
261	Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).

264	\section{Irreducible Sample Analysis}
265	\label{sec:irreducible}
266	
267	The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
268	Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:
269	
270	\begin{itemize}
271	\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
272	\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
273	\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
274	\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
275	\end{itemize}
276	
277	Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
278	Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
279	The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
280	This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
281	
282	Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
283	However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
284	This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
285	The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

392	\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
393	Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}0.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).

395	This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
396	Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.
397	
398	\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
399	All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}0.078$), confirming that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
400	The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}0.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
401	The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).
402	
403	\paragraph{Interpretation.}
404	These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
405	The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
406	The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
407	In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
408	
409	\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
410	Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
411	Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.
412	
413	However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%), indicating that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
414	The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
415	This is consistent with Python's execution model: exception tracebacks and assertion comparisons appear near the end of the trace but are preceded by the final function call frames, placing them typically 300--500 tokens from the terminus rather than at the absolute end.
416	
417	The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
418	The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) confirms that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

624	\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
625	\label{sec:robustness_analysis}
626	
627	The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
628	Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
629	Two of three DeepSeek seeds match Qwen-level accuracy (99.33\%); the outlier (seed 123, 91.09\%) we hypothesize reflects LoRA initialization sensitivity landing in a suboptimal basin (fail recall = 70.5\%, though direct evidence is lacking), not a failure of the exception signal itself; even this outlier outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp.
630	The VOTA cross-model gap is confounded by two factors: (1)~tokenizer efficiency (the DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus Qwen's 1{,}929, causing 91.7\% of training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window; content-aware truncation preferentially removes the terminal structured prompt, preserving the verdict label but truncating trace content) and (2)~base model capability differences, consistent with findings that SFT generalization depends on pretrain quality \citep{yang2024generalization}.
631	The two factors cannot be disentangled in the current experimental design.
632	Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
633	The resulting 0.56pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
634	The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal; for smaller models, training stability (multi-seed selection, warmup schedules) is a secondary but addressable concern.

\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
\label{sec:vota_algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
\label{alg:vota}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\IF{no exception events found}
  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
\ENDIF
\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
\RETURN $V$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{VOTA Trace Examples}
\label{sec:vota_examples}

We provide two representative VOTA trace examples illustrating the fail and pass cases.
In the fail case, the exception event provides an unambiguous fault signal.
In the pass case, the absence of an exception event combined with a matching assertion point confirms correct execution.

\paragraph{Fail example.}
A \texttt{ZeroDivisionError} triggers an \texttt{[ERROR]} event, providing a direct fault signal that is sufficient for the model to predict \texttt{fail}.

## Function
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

## Test Input
divide(1, 0)

## Expected Output
inf

## VOTA Trace
[ERROR] ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

## Verdict
fail
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\paragraph{Pass example.}
No exception is raised, and the assertion point confirms that the actual output matches the expected value.

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
## Function
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

## Test Input
add(2, 3)

## Expected Output
5

## VOTA Trace
[LOOP] No loops detected.
[ASSERT] actual=5, expected=5

## Verdict
pass
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

These examples illustrate the core asymmetry exploited by the \texttt{exception\_only} condition: fail cases produce an explicit \texttt{[ERROR]} event, while pass cases are characterized by its absence.
This binary signal (presence vs.\ absence of an exception) is sufficient for near-perfect verdict prediction.

\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}

The VOTA cross-model gap (14.96pp, Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}; confounded by tokenizer-driven truncation; 91.7\% of DeepSeek training samples were affected) is driven by a training-time truncation asymmetry.
The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.

A post-hoc group analysis provides directional evidence: partitioning DeepSeek VOTA test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}0.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that DeepSeek VOTA achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}, in contrast to Qwen VOTA, which achieves 100\% fail recall.

Seed robustness diverges across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), while DeepSeek shows bimodal behavior: seeds 42 and 456 achieve 99.33\% (fail recall = 100\%), seed 123 yields 91.09\% (fail recall = 70.5\%).
Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).

\section{Irreducible Sample Analysis}
\label{sec:irreducible}

The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
\end{itemize}

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.

Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}0.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).
The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}0.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}0.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.

\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}0.078$), confirming that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}0.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.

However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%), indicating that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
This is consistent with Python's execution model: exception tracebacks and assertion comparisons appear near the end of the trace but are preceded by the final function call frames, placing them typically 300--500 tokens from the terminus rather than at the absolute end.

The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) confirms that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

To test whether exception-based verdict prediction generalizes beyond LLM-generated solutions, we evaluate on DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench}, a dataset of human-written programs with synthetically injected bugs (single-point mutations such as operator replacement, variable misuse, and missing statements).
After filtering for executable Python samples with valid traces, we retain 426 samples with a near-balanced class distribution (majority baseline: 51.4\%).

Table~\ref{tab:debugbench} shows that the component ranking from the main experiments is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} (100.00\%) $\geq$ VOTA (99.77\%) $>$ \texttt{no\_trace} (96.71\%).
The \texttt{exception\_only} condition achieves perfect accuracy, confirming that the exception-based representation generalizes to a different fault distribution without degradation.

The absolute margins are much narrower than on the main dataset: the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline already achieves 96.71\% (compared to 75.13\% on HumanEval+MBPP), leaving only 3.29pp of headroom for trace-based improvement.
This ceiling effect reflects a fundamental difference in fault characteristics: DebugBench bugs are synthetically injected single-point mutations, which produce code that is structurally dissimilar from the original correct solution; a model can often identify the fault from source code alone.
In contrast, the HumanEval+MBPP solutions are LLM-generated, producing natural errors (logic mistakes, edge-case failures) where the faulty and correct solutions may be structurally similar, making code-only verdict prediction substantially harder.

These results support exception-based verdict prediction as a generalizable approach: the method does not degrade on an out-of-distribution dataset, and the exception dominance ranking (exception\_only $\geq$ VOTA $>$ no\_trace) is consistent across both datasets. However, the narrow DebugBench margins are insufficient to independently validate trace importance.
The 24.70pp trace lift on the main dataset (no\_trace 75.13\% $\to$ exception\_only 99.83\%) remains the primary evidence for the value of exception-based trace signals.

\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
\label{sec:robustness_analysis}

The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
Two of three DeepSeek seeds match Qwen-level accuracy (99.33\%); the outlier (seed 123, 91.09\%) we hypothesize reflects LoRA initialization sensitivity landing in a suboptimal basin (fail recall = 70.5\%, though direct evidence is lacking), not a failure of the exception signal itself; even this outlier outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp.
The VOTA cross-model gap is confounded by two factors: (1)~tokenizer efficiency (the DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus Qwen's 1{,}929, causing 91.7\% of training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window; content-aware truncation preferentially removes the terminal structured prompt, preserving the verdict label but truncating trace content) and (2)~base model capability differences, consistent with findings that SFT generalization depends on pretrain quality \citep{yang2024generalization}.
The two factors cannot be disentangled in the current experimental design.
Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
The resulting 0.56pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal; for smaller models, training stability (multi-seed selection, warmup schedules) is a secondary but addressable concern.

%% ============================================================
\section{Training Dynamics and Loss Decoupling}
\label{sec:training_dynamics}

The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results reveal two instructive training dynamics.
First, epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in 2/3 seeds: seed 42 peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), seed 123 degrades from 91.43\% to 91.09\% ($-$0.34pp), while seed 456 shows no epoch degradation (99.33\% at both epoch~1 and epoch~3).
Early stopping may yield marginal gains for some seeds, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp) compared to the seed effect (8.24pp between seeds 42 and 123).

Second, seeds 123 and 456 converge to nearly identical final training losses (0.122 and 0.123 respectively), yet their accuracies differ by 8.24pp (91.09\% vs.\ 99.33\%).
The critical difference lies in fail recall: seeds 42 and 456 achieve 100\%, while seed 123 achieves only 70.5\%. The LoRA initialization in seed 123 fails to learn the exception$\to$fail mapping for a substantial fraction of failing samples, even though the per-token loss appears converged.
This demonstrates that token-level training loss can mask fundamental differences in sample-level classification ability, suggesting a parallel to the eval-loss/accuracy decoupling observed in DeepSeek VOTA (where eval loss rose 65\% from epoch 1 to 3 while accuracy improved by 6.3pp) at the training phase.
The practical recommendation is twofold: (1)~use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training or evaluation loss, and (2)~for deployment on smaller models, train multiple seeds and select the best, as a single run may not reliably converge to the correct classification boundary.

\paragraph{Format collapse, not semantic failure.}
The 100 errors of seed 123 are not semantic failures but generation format collapse: on inputs exceeding 4,000 characters (those containing verbose locals dumps), the model echoes trace content instead of emitting a verdict token, while achieving zero errors on shorter inputs.
This indicates that the LoRA initialization of seed 123 specifically compromises long-context format compliance rather than exception signal comprehension, further supporting the robustness advantage of compact \texttt{exception\_only} inputs.

The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, but is consistent with a performance limit associated with the high trace truncation rate (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}): the model progressively extracts signal from samples with intact trace content but cannot fully compensate for the information loss in the truncated majority.
The 84.45\% accuracy reflects a combination of trace information loss and model capability constraints.

\section{Deduplication Statistics}
\label{sec:dedup_stats}

Table~\ref{tab:dedup} reports the duplication rates across trace formats.
Because multiple passing solutions to the same problem produce identical (input, output) pairs in the \texttt{exception\_only} format (correct executions raise no exceptions, so the trace content is the same regardless of the solution's internal logic), the dataset contains duplicate rows.
Train--test input overlap is zero (split by problem ID), so no information leakage occurs.
The high duplication in \texttt{exception\_only} does not affect our experimental conclusions: after deduplication the training set still contains 2,858 unique samples and the test set 607, providing sufficient coverage for the 591-problem benchmark.

\paragraph{Problem-level partitioning and sensitivity analysis.}
Data is partitioned at the problem level: 472 training problems and 119 test problems, with zero crossover.
Duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem (up to 10 solutions each), not from cross-problem overlap.
To verify that deduplication does not alter any finding, we ran a sensitivity analysis across all 19 experimental conditions (7 trace formats $\times$ 4 models, minus conditions not run): deduplication produces a 0.00pp accuracy delta in every case.
This confirms that duplicate samples neither inflate nor deflate accuracy, because duplicates share the same ground-truth label and the model's prediction is deterministic at inference time.
The \texttt{exception\_only} test set contains 48.99\% duplicate inputs due to representation compactness; all confidence intervals treat samples as independent Bernoulli trials.

\label{sec:regex_baselines}

To establish a non-learning upper bound, we evaluate six regex-based baselines on the \texttt{exception\_only} test set ($N{=}1{,}190$) and two format-specific baselines on VOTA and \texttt{full\_trace} inputs.

The strongest legitimate baseline (B4, 93.61\%) applies regex pattern-matching on Python exception class names (e.g., \texttt{ValueError}, \texttt{TypeError}).
Its errors concentrate on 8 boundary samples where a \texttt{ValueError} is raised inside a \texttt{try/except} block and caught; the program passes despite an exception occurring in the trace.
SFT \texttt{exception\_only} correctly classifies 6 of these 8 samples, indicating that the model learns the semantic distinction between caught (benign) and uncaught (fault-indicating) exceptions.
B5 (99.33\%) achieves near-SFT accuracy but relies on the deterministic presence of a format marker in pass-class traces, which is an artifact of the trace preprocessing pipeline rather than a generalizable signal; McNemar test vs.\ SFT yields $p{=}0.041$, confirming a statistically significant difference.

Table~\ref{tab:regex_cross_format} compares SFT and the best applicable regex baseline for each trace format.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Execution Traces for Code LLMs.}
TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} scaled trace-augmented training to 2.6M samples; \citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility task- and format-dependent, which we extend by identifying exception events as the dominant signal.
NExT \citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} used trace chain-of-thought for repair and execution reasoning; \citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, supporting our density finding.
\citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained on execution traces; \citet{chen2024selfdebug} demonstrated LLM self-debugging from execution results.
CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, extended to 19 languages \citep{xu2025cruxevalx}, established execution reasoning benchmarks.
None decompose which trace components contribute to \emph{classification} accuracy.

\paragraph{Code Verdict and Patch Classification.}
TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; DeepDFA \citep{steenhoek2024deepdfa} and learned program slicing \citep{yadavally2024slicing} combined classical analysis with deep learning.
In patch correctness, \citet{tian2020patchcorrectness}, CC2Vec \citep{hoang2020cc2vec}, LLM4PatchCorrect \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} (84.4\%), and APPT \citep{appt2024} (79.7\%) developed representation learning of code changes.
Verdict prediction is an instance of the longstanding test oracle problem \citep{barr2015oracle}; oracle generation progressed from ATLAS \citep{watson2020atlas} through retrieval-augmented approaches \citep{yu2022assertion,nashid2023assertion} to TOGA \citep{dinella2022toga}.
FuseFL \citep{widyasari2024fusefl} and \citet{foster2025mutation} demonstrated structured fault signals; the equivalent-mutant problem in mutation testing \citep{papadakis2019mutation} poses an analogous classification challenge to verdict prediction on DebugBench's single-point mutations.
None isolate individual trace components or compare against rule-based baselines.

\paragraph{Fault Localization.}
Spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL) ranks program elements by suspiciousness from test spectra \citep{abreu2007accuracy,jones2002visualization,wong2014dstar}; recent LLM-based approaches \citep{kang2024autofl,qin2024agentfl,widyasari2024llm4fl,mukherjee2025llmfl} share our insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal.
Verdict prediction is a prerequisite to FL (determining \emph{whether} a fault exists before localizing \emph{where}), and both exploit the same signal type at different granularities.

\paragraph{Trace Compression and Selection.}
TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} use selective trace extraction; RepairAgent \citep{bouzenia2025repairagent} and Agentless \citep{xia2024agentless} incorporate execution feedback in repair workflows, as do SWE-agent \citep{yang2024sweagent} and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands}, which close the loop between code generation, execution, and iterative revision.
Automated log analysis \citep{he2021loganalysis} provides parsing techniques for extracting structured events from build logs and test outputs, a prerequisite for feeding such signals to downstream models.
In the prompt compression literature, LLMLingua \citep{jiang2023llmlingua} and Selective Context \citep{li2023selectivecontext} showed that pruning low-information tokens from LLM inputs preserves downstream accuracy, corroborating our finding that compact trace formats outperform verbose ones.
\citet{haque2025traces} found raw traces provide limited repair benefit; SWE-bench \citep{jimenez2024swebench} provides a realistic benchmark.
Our approximate decomposition (gradient dilution ${\sim}$24\% vs.\ information overload ${\sim}$76\%) provides the first quantitative framework for \emph{why} compression helps, complementing these methods' focus on \emph{how}.

\paragraph{Calibration and Defect Prediction.}
Neural network calibration \citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration,spiess2025calibration}, studies confidence-correctness alignment; our ECE ${<}$ 0.007 suggests compact inputs improve calibration.
Just-in-time defect prediction \citep{kamei2013large,hoang2019deepjit,pornprasit2021jitline} shares our fault detection motivation but operates on code change features rather than traces.

\paragraph{Training Efficiency and Data Selection.}
Curriculum learning \citep{bengio2009curriculum}, dataset cartography via training dynamics \citep{swayamdipta2020cartography}, and data selection methods \citep{sachdeva2024dataefficient,xie2023doremi} show that data quality and ordering improve convergence, consistent with our finding that compact exceptions enable rapid convergence while verbose traces trap the model in oscillation.

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
Yet feeding thousands of trace lines to a model can be no better than feeding none: the diagnostic signal drowns in routine execution steps.
\emph{Which trace components actually carry the signal that matters?}

Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks.
\emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, enabling controlled component ablation.
As fault detection, the model need not simulate execution, only determine whether something went wrong---and if that signal is concentrated in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.

We test this hypothesis through the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2025coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.
The results are striking: complete traces (${\sim}$80\%) underperform a single compact component (${\geq}$99\%) despite containing strictly more information---a direct demonstration that information density, not quantity, determines learning efficiency.

\textbf{Exception events alone achieve ${\geq}$99.83\% verdict accuracy on three of four models (${\geq}$99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds; CodeLlama-13B seed 123 reaches 100\%).}
DeepSeek-6.7B is the exception: its 3-seed mean is 96.58\% ($\pm$4.76pp) due to one seed exhibiting format collapse (fail recall = 70.5\%), though even this outlier outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp.
This near-perfect accuracy holds from 1.5B to 13B parameters, while the code-only baseline (\texttt{no\_trace}) varies from 67.3\% to 76.5\% with strong scale dependence.
Training dynamics expose the mechanism (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}): \texttt{exception\_only} converges to 99.33\% within 50 training steps and saturates at 99.83\% by step 150, while even \texttt{full\_trace} with label-only loss (gradient dilution eliminated) oscillates between 82\% and 89\% across the entire training without stable convergence, consistent with overfitting to spurious patterns in verbose content.

Adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit and can degrade performance: VOTA (3-seed mean 99.05\%) underperforms \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) on Qwen-7B, with the gap reaching 14.96pp on DeepSeek due to tokenizer-driven truncation.
The performance gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\sim}$76\%) and gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) on Qwen-7B (3 seeds).
A tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens, with \texttt{tail\_2048} recovering 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy.
Even on silent logic errors (55.5\% of failures), \texttt{exception\_only} maintains 100\% recall because test assertions generate exception events.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Information density determines SFT learning efficiency}: training dynamics directly show that denser trace components learn faster and more stably---\texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} with label-only loss oscillates (82--89\%) without stable convergence. Seed variance negatively correlates with input density ($\sigma{=}$0.00 to 1.12), and SFT closes a 6--49pp zero-shot gap across all models (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
\item \textbf{Exception events are the minimal sufficient signal}: ${\geq}$99.83\% on three of four models, ${\geq}$99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds (1.5B--13B, three families), with ${\sim}$91\% semantic rather than format-driven (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}, \S\ref{sec:nomarker}). Cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the ranking, though margins narrow from ceiling effects (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).
\item \textbf{Approximate density decomposition (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds)}: The performance gap decomposes into gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) and information overload (${\sim}$76\%), implying content selection matters more than loss engineering. A budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tail tokens (\S\ref{sec:density}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy (Qwen-7B; cross-model verification in progress)}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertions) individually achieve ${\geq}$99\%; Tier~2 (loop compression) reaches 86.1\%, still +10.9pp over no trace (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{enumerate}
